content.text:
**None of the conversion is taxable for 2025. The taxable amount is $0, and the pro-rata rule doesn't apply.**

**Why:** Daniel put a $7,000 nondeductible 2025 contribution into his traditional IRA (SYN-15870003) on 11 Feb 2025. He converted the same $7,000 to his Roth IRA (SYN-15870004) on 14 Feb 2025. That leaves no earnings to tax. The pro-rata rule weighs his basis against the year-end value of *all* his traditional, SEP and SIMPLE IRAs. At 31 Dec 2025 he had only this one, and it held $0. So the whole $7,000 conversion comes out of basis:

| Form 8606 line | Value |
|---|---|
| 1 Nondeductible contribution for 2025 | $7,000 |
| 2 Basis from earlier years | $0 |
| 3 Total basis | $7,000 |
| 6 Value of all his traditional IRAs at 31 Dec 2025 | $0 |
| 8 Amount converted | $7,000 |
| 10 Nontaxable share | 1.000 |
| 13 Nontaxable part | $7,000 |
| **14 Basis carried to 2026** | **$0** |
| **18 Taxable amount** | **$0** |

**What to watch:**
- **The 401(k) doesn't count.** His old employer's 401(k) (SYN-15870002, $178,338.60 at year-end) is an employer plan, not an IRA, so it stays out of the calculation. If he ever rolls it into an IRA, pre-tax money would enter the calculation for later backdoor conversions.
- **The 1099-R overstates the taxable amount.** It shows box 2a "taxable amount" as $7,000, with 2b "taxable amount not determined" checked. Form 8606 is what brings the taxable amount down to $0, but only if it's filed with the 2025 joint return. As of 15 April that's due that day, so the preparer needs to confirm it's been filed or extended, or amend if it was left off.

**CRM entries for HH-1587, all dated 15 April 2026:**
- **Note SB-1587-01:** the finding, the figures it turns on, and the 401(k) rollover point.
- **Task SB-1587-02:** you review and send the client message below. I've drafted it but not sent it, so it isn't logged as sent.
- **Task SB-1587-03:** Daniel and the tax preparer file Form 8606 with the 2025 return.
- **Task SB-1587-04:** the firm gets a copy of the filed 8606 and updates Daniel's IRA basis in the tax profile to $0 as of 31 Dec 2025.

**Draft message to the client:**

> Dear Sofia and Daniel,
>
> As part of your 2025 review we looked at Daniel's backdoor Roth conversion. Daniel contributed $7,000 to his traditional IRA in February 2025 as a nondeductible contribution and converted the same $7,000 to his Roth IRA three days later. Because that traditional IRA was empty at the end of 2025, and Daniel had no other traditional IRAs, none of the conversion should be taxable income for 2025. His former employer's 401(k) doesn't count toward this calculation.
>
> One thing to watch: the 2025 Form 1099-R from the IRA custodian shows the full $7,000 as a distribution and doesn't work out how much of it is taxable. The $0 result depends on Form 8606 being filed with your 2025 joint return, reporting the $7,000 nondeductible contribution and the $7,000 conversion. Please make sure your tax preparer has the 1099-R and knows about Form 8606. Today is the filing deadline, so please check with them that your return has been filed or extended. We don't prepare tax returns, so your preparer should confirm the final figures. Once it's filed, please send us a copy of Form 8606 for our records.
>
> Finally, if you ever think about moving Daniel's 401(k) into an IRA, please talk to us first. It could make future backdoor Roth conversions partly taxable.
>
> Best regards,
